name: Dextromethorphan/Bupropion (Auvelity)
summary: Oral antidepressant for major depressive disorder in adults that combines NMDA-modulating dextromethorphan with bupropion. Not for children or teens; carries a suicidality boxed warning and seizure risk.
description: Auvelity is a combination of dextromethorphan and bupropion used to treat major depressive disorder (MDD) in adults. Dextromethorphan modulates glutamate (via NMDA and sigma-1 receptors) and serotonin, while bupropion increases dopamine and norepinephrine and strongly inhibits CYP2D6, which boosts dextromethorphan levels. Compared with traditional antidepressants, some patients experience symptom improvement as early as 1 to 2 weeks, with continued benefit over 4 to 6 weeks. Important risks include suicidal thoughts and behaviors in younger adults, seizures, hypertension, and neuropsychiatric reactions. It is not approved for pediatric use.
patient_summary: Auvelity is a newer antidepressant for adults with major depression. It combines dextromethorphan (a cough-suppressant medicine at higher, brain-active doses) with bupropion (an antidepressant that also boosts dopamine and norepinephrine). Many people start to notice mood and energy improvements within 1 to 2 weeks, with more benefit over a month or longer. Common side effects include dizziness, nausea, dry mouth, sweating, and trouble sleeping. Serious risks include suicidal thoughts in young adults, high blood pressure, and seizures—especially in people with seizure risk or eating disorders. It’s not for children or teens and should not be used with other bupropion products or monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs).

metadata.pharmacologic_category: Antidepressant, Dopamine/Norepinephrine-Reuptake Inhibitor; NMDA Receptor Antagonist

primary_indications: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD), unipolar, in adults

linked_conditions.context: FDA-approved for treatment of unipolar major depressive disorder in adults. Considered when patients have not responded adequately to prior antidepressants or when a faster onset of effect is desired.

Sometimes considered in adults with inadequate response to multiple antidepressant trials, as a non-SSRI/SNRI option with glutamatergic modulation. Must carefully evaluate seizure risk and drug interactions.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity (eg, anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, delayed hypersensitivity) to dextromethorphan, bupropion, or any component of the formulation
Current or prior diagnosis of bulimia nervosa or anorexia nervosa
Seizure disorder or a history of seizures
Patients undergoing abrupt discontinuation of alcohol, benzodiazepines, barbiturates, or antiseizure drugs
Use with or within 14 days of stopping monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) including linezolid or IV methylene blue
Initiation in a patient receiving linezolid or IV methylene blue
Concurrent use of other bupropion-containing products

efficacy_response.metric: Onset and magnitude of antidepressant response
efficacy_response.patient_text: In clinical trials, many adults taking Auvelity had meaningful improvements in depressive symptoms within 1 to 2 weeks, with continued benefit through 4 to 6 weeks. Overall, it performed better than placebo and better than bupropion alone on standard depression rating scales.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Well absorbed orally; extended-release formulation provides sustained exposure.
pharmacokinetics.bioavailability: Not fully defined; clinically effective at fixed-dose combination.
pharmacokinetics.onset: Initial antidepressant effects may be seen within 1 to 2 weeks; full effect often requires 4 to 6 weeks.
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Bupropion: ~2 hours; hydroxybupropion: ~3 hours; other active metabolites: ~4 hours; dextromethorphan: ~3 hours.
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Bupropion: ~15 hours; hydroxybupropion: ~35 hours; other active metabolites: ~33–44 hours; dextromethorphan: ~22 hours.
pharmacokinetics.duration_ER: Sustained effect over 24-hour dosing interval at steady state.
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Bupropion: extensive hepatic metabolism to 3 active metabolites (hydroxybupropion, erythrohydroxybupropion, threohydroxybupropion). Dextromethorphan: primarily via CYP2D6 to dextrorphan. Bupropion strongly inhibits CYP2D6, increasing dextromethorphan exposure.
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Bupropion: ~87% in urine and ~10% in feces, mostly as metabolites; ~0.5% as unchanged drug. Dextromethorphan: urinary excretion of metabolites; higher proportion of unchanged drug in CYP2D6 poor metabolizers.
pharmacokinetics.protein_binding: Bupropion: ~84%; hydroxybupropion similar; other metabolites about half that; dextromethorphan: 60–70%.
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: May be administered with or without food; no major clinically relevant food effect reported.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Auvelity is approved for adults with unipolar major depressive disorder. It targets depression through multiple brain pathways (glutamate, monoamines) and may work faster for some patients than traditional antidepressants.
items: Major Depressive Disorder (unipolar) in adults: Depressed mood, low energy, loss of interest, changes in sleep and appetite, difficulty concentrating, and feelings of worthlessness or guilt.
Patients who have not responded adequately to prior antidepressant trials may be considered for Auvelity as an alternative mechanism option.
Some clinicians consider Auvelity when a potentially faster onset of antidepressant effect is desired compared with SSRI/SNRI monotherapy.
off_label: Treatment-resistant depression in adults who have failed multiple prior antidepressant trials (specialist use, not formally approved)
Potential future use in other mood or neuropsychiatric conditions is under study, but not currently approved.

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Experiences vary, but these are common patterns reported by adults taking Auvelity:

quotes: I noticed my mood felt a bit lighter within the first couple of weeks.
Getting out of bed and starting my day didn’t feel quite as impossible.
The constant emotional ‘weight’ started to lift a little faster than with my last antidepressant.
My motivation slowly came back—I actually want to do things again.
The dark, hopeless thoughts eased up and I could think more clearly.
I still have bad days, but they’re fewer and less intense.
I feel a bit dizzy or woozy, especially after a dose.
Nausea was rough for the first week, then it settled down.
My mouth is dry and I sweat more than usual.
items.note: Dizziness and nausea are among the most common side effects, especially when starting or increasing the dose.

quotes: My sleep got more broken once I was taking it twice a day.
I felt more keyed up and anxious instead of calmer.
Some dark, scary thoughts popped up again when the dose changed.
items.note: Insomnia, anxiety, and suicidal thoughts can worsen or emerge, especially early in treatment or when changing doses—these changes need immediate attention.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Auvelity is designed to act on depression pathways more quickly than traditional antidepressants, although it still requires time to work.
key_points: 1–2 weeks: Many people notice early improvements in mood, energy, or interest, though not full remission.
4–6 weeks: Typical timeframe to see full antidepressant benefit in clinical trials.
Dosing schedule: Start once daily in the morning for 3 days, then usually increase to twice daily, at least 8 hours apart.
Long half-lives: Bupropion and its active metabolites have long half-lives (15–44 hours), so missed doses may not lead to immediate withdrawal but can gradually reduce benefit.

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.metric: Symptom Improvement on Depression Rating Scales
sections.text: In clinical studies of adults with major depressive disorder, Auvelity led to greater improvements on standard depression rating scales compared with placebo and with bupropion alone. Some patients experienced meaningful symptom relief as early as week 1, with continued improvement through weeks 4 to 6.
sections.clinical_details: Phase 2/3 randomized, double-blind trials compared Auvelity to placebo or bupropion sustained-release in adults with moderate to severe MDD. Patients receiving Auvelity showed significantly larger reductions in depressive symptoms and higher response and remission rates at multiple time points. The combination leverages glutamatergic modulation via dextromethorphan and dopaminergic/noradrenergic effects via bupropion, with bupropion’s CYP2D6 inhibition increasing dextromethorphan exposure.

citation.authors: Iosifescu DV, Tabuteau H, et al.
citation.title: Efficacy and safety of dextromethorphan-bupropion in major depressive disorder
citation.journal: Randomized controlled trials of Auvelity in adults with MDD

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Suicidality boxed warning: Antidepressants can increase suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults.
sections.black_box: Antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in pediatric and young adult patients in short-term studies. Monitor closely for clinical worsening and emergence of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in all patients starting or changing Auvelity, especially during the first 1–2 months and around dose changes. Auvelity is not approved for use in pediatric patients.
other: Seizure risk: Auvelity (through its bupropion component) increases the risk of seizures in a dose-related manner. It is contraindicated in patients with a seizure disorder, eating disorders (anorexia/bulimia), or undergoing abrupt withdrawal from alcohol, benzodiazepines, barbiturates, or antiseizure medications.

Hypertension: Can elevate blood pressure and cause hypertension, even in patients without prior high blood pressure. Risk is higher when combined with MAOIs, nicotine replacement, or other dopaminergic/noradrenergic drugs.

Mania/hypomania: May trigger manic, mixed, or hypomanic episodes in people with bipolar disorder or at risk for bipolar disorder. Screen for bipolar history before starting and avoid using Auvelity to treat bipolar depression.

Neuropsychiatric effects: Serious neuropsychiatric reactions have been reported with bupropion, including delusions, hallucinations, psychosis, paranoia, confusion, and concentration problems. Dextromethorphan overdose can also cause toxic psychosis, stupor, and hyperexcitability.
Ocular effects: Mild pupillary dilation can precipitate an acute narrow-angle glaucoma attack in susceptible individuals. Patients with untreated narrow angles should be evaluated before starting.

Renal and hepatic impairment: Use with caution in kidney or liver disease. Dose reduction is recommended for moderate renal impairment, and use is not recommended in severe renal impairment (eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m²) or Child-Pugh C liver disease.

Abuse/misuse: Taking higher-than-prescribed doses of bupropion-containing products has been associated with agitation, excitement, euphoria, and increased seizure risk. Dextromethorphan also has misuse potential at high doses.
patient_counseling: Watch for new or worsening depression, suicidal thoughts, or sudden behavior changes, especially in the first 1–2 months or after dose changes. Involve family or trusted supports to help monitor.
Do not take Auvelity if you have a seizure disorder, an eating disorder (like anorexia or bulimia), or are suddenly stopping alcohol, benzodiazepines, barbiturates, or seizure medicines.
Check blood pressure before starting and during treatment. Tell your clinician if you have headaches, chest pain, or feel your heart pounding.
Tell your clinician if you or a family member has bipolar disorder, mania, or psychosis; Auvelity is not approved for bipolar depression.
Do not combine Auvelity with MAOIs or other bupropion-containing medications. Always show your prescriber and pharmacist a full list of your medications.
If you develop eye pain, changes in vision, or halos around lights, seek urgent eye care.
If you experience a seizure while on Auvelity, stop the medication and seek emergency care. Do not restart unless your clinician specifically directs you to.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common side effects are dizziness and nausea. Other frequent issues include dry mouth, sweating, diarrhea, constipation, decreased appetite, insomnia, and sexual side effects.
plain_language_list: Sexual side effects (changes in desire, arousal, or orgasm)

common.patient_note: Dizziness often occurs when starting or increasing the dose. Standing up slowly, staying hydrated, and avoiding driving or operating machinery until you know how you react can help.
Nausea is usually worst in the first days to weeks and may improve over time. Taking with food (if tolerated) and drinking small sips of water can help.
Keep water or sugar-free candy handy for dry mouth. Sweating may be more noticeable during exercise or at night.
Some people feel more tired, others more wired or have trouble sleeping. Dose timing (earlier in the day) and overall sleep habits often need adjustment.

Changes in sexual desire, arousal, or orgasm can occur. Unlike some SSRIs, bupropion-containing regimens may have less sexual dysfunction in many patients, but problems can still occur and should be discussed openly.
Bowel habits may change in either direction. Appetite can decrease modestly; sudden or large weight changes should be reported.

serious: Suicidal thoughts or behaviors: New or worsening depression, suicidal thinking, or self-harm behavior—especially in younger adults or early in treatment. Requires urgent contact with a clinician or emergency services.
Seizures: Sudden loss of consciousness, stiffening, jerking movements, or confusion afterward. Stop Auvelity and seek emergency care.
Severe hypertension: Markedly elevated blood pressure, severe headache, chest pain, shortness of breath, or neurologic symptoms.
Mania/hypomania: Abnormally elevated or irritable mood, racing thoughts, decreased need for sleep, impulsive or risky behaviors.
Psychosis/neuropsychiatric reactions: Hallucinations, delusions, paranoia, confusion, or unusual behavior changes.
Allergic or severe skin reactions: Rash, hives, blistering, peeling skin, or signs of Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
Acute angle-closure glaucoma: Sudden eye pain, vision changes, halos around lights, red eye—requires urgent eye care.

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Auvelity has important interactions because bupropion strongly inhibits CYP2D6 and dextromethorphan is serotonergic and glutamatergic. Some combinations are absolutely contraindicated.

items.with: Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitors (MAOIs) including phenelzine, tranylcypromine, isocarboxazid, selegiline, linezolid, IV methylene blue
items.risk: Serious, potentially life-threatening reactions including hypertensive crisis and serotonin syndrome.
items.action: Contraindicated. Allow at least 14 days between stopping an MAOI and starting Auvelity, and 14 days between stopping Auvelity and starting an MAOI.

items.with: Other bupropion-containing products (Wellbutrin, Zyban, Aplenzin, Forfivo, etc.)
items.risk: Higher total bupropion exposure and a marked increase in seizure risk.
items.action: Do NOT combine Auvelity with other bupropion products.

items.with: Drugs that lower seizure threshold (antipsychotics, antidepressants, theophylline, systemic corticosteroids, stimulants, cocaine, anorexiants, hypoglycemics, abrupt withdrawal from alcohol or benzodiazepines)
items.action: Use extreme caution or avoid. Carefully weigh risks vs benefits and monitor closely if combination cannot be avoided.

items.with: CYP2D6 substrates (TCAs, many SSRIs and SNRIs, some antipsychotics, beta-blockers, certain opioids like codeine and tramadol, tamoxifen)
items.risk: Bupropion is a strong CYP2D6 inhibitor, increasing levels of these drugs and altering their effects (including increased side effects or toxicity, or reduced efficacy for prodrugs like codeine and tamoxifen).
items.action: Consider dose reduction of the interacting drug, close monitoring, and in some cases alternative therapies not dependent on CYP2D6.

items.with: Other serotonergic agents (SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, triptans, tramadol, fentanyl, lithium, St. John’s wort, tryptophan)
items.risk: Increased risk of serotonin syndrome (agitation, confusion, sweating, tremor, fever).
items.action: Use with caution. Educate patients on serotonin syndrome symptoms and seek urgent care if they occur.

items.with: Nicotine replacement (patch, gum, lozenges) or other noradrenergic agents
items.risk: Additive increases in blood pressure and heart rate.
items.action: Monitor blood pressure more frequently; adjust doses or consider alternative smoking cessation options.

items.with: Alcohol, benzodiazepines, barbiturates, and antiseizure drugs (around discontinuation)
items.risk: Abrupt discontinuation of these agents while on Auvelity is contraindicated due to seizure risk.
items.action: Taper these agents carefully under medical supervision before considering Auvelity, or avoid Auvelity if abrupt discontinuation is necessary.

sections.heading: Stopping or Changing Auvelity Safely
sections.text: There is limited direct data on withdrawal from Auvelity, but antidepressant best practices suggest tapering to reduce the risk of discontinuation symptoms and detect symptom relapse.
key_points: Bupropion: Has minimal serotonergic activity, so classic SSRI-type discontinuation symptoms (brain zaps, flu-like symptoms) are less common.
Dextromethorphan: Little is known about withdrawal at antidepressant doses. As a precaution, tapering over at least 2–4 weeks is recommended after more than 3 weeks of treatment.
General tapering: Gradually reduce the dose over 2–4 weeks (or longer for sensitive patients or long-term use) to minimize withdrawal symptoms and monitor for return of depression.
Slower tapers: Consider tapering over 4+ weeks or even several months in patients with previous discontinuation problems, high doses, or long-term use.
If severe symptoms occur: Resume the prior dose and taper more slowly rather than stopping abruptly.

Switching antidepressants: Cross-titration over 1–4 weeks is common for most switches, but is contraindicated when switching to or from an MAOI. In those cases, strict washout periods (usually 14 days) are required.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Auvelity is given as a fixed-dose extended-release tablet. Dosing is straightforward in adults with normal kidney and liver function, but must be modified in some patients.

adult.mdd_initial: Dextromethorphan 45 mg / bupropion 105 mg once daily in the morning for the first 3 days.
adult.mdd_titration: After 3 days, increase to 45 mg / 105 mg twice daily, at least 8 hours apart (typically morning and early evening).
adult.mdd_max: Maximum daily dose: dextromethorphan 90 mg / bupropion 210 mg (one tablet twice daily).
adult.cyp2d6_poor_metabolizers: 45 mg / 105 mg once daily in the morning (avoid twice-daily dosing due to higher dextromethorphan exposure).
adult.renal_moderate: eGFR 30–59 mL/min/1.73 m²: 45 mg / 105 mg once daily in the morning.
adult.renal_severe: eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m²: Use not recommended (not studied).
adult.hepatic_mild_moderate: Child-Pugh class A or B: No dose adjustment required, but use with caution.
adult.hepatic_severe: Child-Pugh class C: Use not recommended (not studied).
adult.timing: Swallow tablets whole with or without food; do not crush, divide, or chew. Separate doses by at least 8 hours and avoid taking close to bedtime to reduce insomnia.

sections.simple_explanation: Most adults start with one tablet in the morning for 3 days, then increase to one tablet twice a day (about 8 hours apart). People with certain genetic traits (CYP2D6 poor metabolizers) or moderate kidney problems usually stay on once-daily dosing. The tablets are extended-release and must be swallowed whole.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, and Special Groups
sections.text: Auvelity has limited human data in pregnancy and breastfeeding and important cautions in certain medical conditions.
sections.pregnancy: Pregnant patients were excluded from Auvelity clinical trials, and participants were required to use contraception. Bupropion and its metabolites cross the placenta; combined use with dextromethorphan leads to higher dextromethorphan exposure than dextromethorphan alone, and animal studies have shown adverse outcomes with such combinations. Use during pregnancy is not recommended. When possible, alternative treatments with more established safety data in pregnancy should be considered.
sections.lactation: Bupropion and its active metabolites are present in breast milk; excretion of dextromethorphan in human milk is not known. Due to the potential for neurotoxicity in the breastfed infant and higher dextromethorphan exposure with this combination, breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment and for 5 days after the last dose.
sections.pediatrics: Auvelity is not approved for pediatric use. Antidepressants, including Auvelity, carry a boxed warning for increased risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults. Use in those under 18 should generally be avoided outside of research or highly specialized settings.
sections.geriatrics: Older adults may be more susceptible to dizziness, falls, blood pressure changes, and neuropsychiatric effects. Start at the standard adult dose but monitor closely, especially for dizziness, confusion, and blood pressure changes.
sections.hepatic: In mild or moderate liver impairment (Child-Pugh A or B), no formal dose adjustment is required, but plasma concentrations may be higher; monitor for side effects and consider slower titration. Use is not recommended in severe liver impairment (Child-Pugh C).
sections.renal: In moderate renal impairment (eGFR 30–59 mL/min/1.73 m²), lower the dose to once daily. In severe impairment (eGFR <30), use is not recommended.
sections.reproductive_considerations: Patients planning pregnancy were excluded from clinical trials and were required to use contraception. For patients actively trying to conceive, alternative treatments are generally preferred. Pregnant patients exposed to antidepressants can be referred to the National Pregnancy Registry for Antidepressants for outcome monitoring.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Mood and suicidality: Monitor for worsening depression, suicidal thoughts, and behavior changes at each visit, especially during the first 1–2 months and after dose changes.
Blood pressure: Check before starting and periodically during treatment. Monitor more closely in patients with hypertension or using nicotine replacement or other noradrenergic agents.
Seizure risk factors: Screen for history of seizures, eating disorders, alcohol or sedative dependence, head trauma, or concurrent medications that lower seizure threshold.
Bipolar disorder history: Assess personal and family history of bipolar disorder, mania, hypomania, or psychosis prior to starting; avoid using Auvelity to treat bipolar depression.
Renal and hepatic function: Check baseline kidney and liver function and repeat as clinically indicated, especially in older adults or those with known impairment.
Neuropsychiatric status: Monitor for hallucinations, delusions, paranoia, confusion, or agitation.
Visual symptoms: Ask about eye pain, blurred vision, or visual halos which may signal narrow-angle glaucoma.
Adherence and response: Track changes in depressive symptoms, functioning, sleep, appetite, and overall quality of life.
Concomitant medications: Review medication list regularly for CYP2D6 substrates, other antidepressants, MAOIs, and bupropion-containing products.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Auvelity is currently available as a single fixed-dose extended-release tablet strength.
items: Extended-Release Oral Tablet: Dextromethorphan hydrobromide 45 mg and bupropion hydrochloride 105 mg (Auvelity).
No generic equivalent is currently available in the US.
Tablets must be swallowed whole and should not be crushed, split, or chewed.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Auvelity works through complementary mechanisms. Dextromethorphan acts as an uncompetitive NMDA receptor antagonist, a sigma-1 receptor agonist, and a serotonin reuptake inhibitor, modulating glutamate and serotonin pathways involved in mood regulation. Bupropion is a dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (DNRI) that enhances catecholamine signaling. Bupropion also strongly inhibits CYP2D6, increasing dextromethorphan levels and prolonging its effects. Together, these mechanisms aim to normalize disrupted brain circuits in depression through both monoaminergic and glutamatergic modulation.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Auvelity is an option for adults with unipolar major depressive disorder, particularly when traditional antidepressants have provided incomplete benefit or when a different mechanism of action is desired. It is not a first-line agent for all patients, but may be considered after or alongside SSRIs, SNRIs, or other standard therapies based on patient preference, side effect profiles, and prior treatment history. It is not approved for bipolar depression and should not be used as monotherapy in patients with bipolar disorder due to the risk of mania. Because of seizure risk and important interactions, careful screening and monitoring are essential. Auvelity is not recommended in pregnancy, breastfeeding, pediatric patients, or those with significant seizure risk or severe renal/hepatic impairment.

seo.title: Auvelity (Dextromethorphan/Bupropion): Uses, Dosing, Side Effects & Suicidality Warning
seo.description: Auvelity for major depressive disorder in adults: how it works via NMDA modulation and DNRI effects, dosing (45/105 mg once then twice daily), common side effects, suicidality and seizure risks, drug interactions, pregnancy cautions, and monitoring.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and aligned with current FDA prescribing information for Auvelity, major depression treatment guidelines, and expert recommendations on antidepressant use, suicidality risk, and seizure precautions.

faqs.a: Auvelity is an oral antidepressant approved to treat major depressive disorder (unipolar depression) in adults. It combines dextromethorphan, which modulates glutamate and serotonin, with bupropion, which boosts dopamine and norepinephrine and increases dextromethorphan levels.

Some adults notice early improvements in mood, energy, or interest within 1 to 2 weeks, which is faster than many traditional antidepressants. Full benefit usually emerges over 4 to 6 weeks. Individual responses vary.

faqs.q: What is the boxed warning for Auvelity?
faqs.a: Like all antidepressants, Auvelity carries a boxed warning about increased risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults. It’s not approved for pediatric patients. All patients—especially younger adults—should be monitored closely when starting or changing the dose.

You should not take Auvelity if you have a seizure disorder, a current or past eating disorder (anorexia or bulimia), are abruptly stopping alcohol, benzodiazepines, barbiturates, or seizure medications, are using an MAOI (or have used one in the last 14 days), are using linezolid or IV methylene blue, or are taking other bupropion products. People with severe kidney or liver disease generally should not use it.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects of Auvelity?
faqs.a: The most common side effects are dizziness, nausea, dry mouth, sweating, diarrhea, constipation, decreased appetite, trouble sleeping, fatigue, and sexual side effects. Many are most noticeable when starting or increasing the dose and may improve over time.

Yes. The bupropion component increases the risk of seizures in a dose-related way. The risk is higher if you have a seizure disorder, eating disorder, heavy alcohol or sedative use, or take other medicines that lower seizure threshold. Auvelity is contraindicated in several of these situations. If a seizure occurs while taking Auvelity, the medication should be stopped and urgent medical care sought.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking Auvelity?
faqs.a: Heavy alcohol use or abrupt alcohol withdrawal increases seizure risk with bupropion. While small amounts of alcohol may be tolerated for some people, mixing Auvelity and alcohol is generally discouraged. You should not suddenly stop heavy drinking while on Auvelity without medical supervision because of seizure risk.

faqs.q: Can Auvelity be taken with other antidepressants?
faqs.a: Sometimes Auvelity is combined with other antidepressants, but this increases the complexity of drug interactions, including serotonin syndrome and CYP2D6-related interactions. It must not be combined with MAOIs or other bupropion-containing products. Any combination should be carefully managed by a prescriber experienced with polypharmacy in depression.

faqs.q: Is Auvelity safe during pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Auvelity has limited human data in pregnancy and breastfeeding and is generally not recommended in these situations. Bupropion crosses the placenta and enters breast milk, and dextromethorphan exposure is higher in this combination. Alternative treatments with better-established safety are usually preferred. Patients exposed during pregnancy can enroll in the National Pregnancy Registry for Antidepressants.

faqs.q: What is the usual dose of Auvelity?
faqs.a: Most adults start with one 45 mg/105 mg tablet once daily in the morning for 3 days, then increase to one tablet twice daily, at least 8 hours apart. People with moderate kidney impairment or who are CYP2D6 poor metabolizers usually stay on once-daily dosing. Do not crush, chew, or split the tablets.

faqs.q: Can Auvelity be used in children or teenagers?
faqs.a: No. Auvelity is not approved for use in pediatric patients. Antidepressants, including Auvelity, can increase the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults, so alternative approaches with established pediatric data are preferred.

faqs.q: What should I do if I miss a dose of Auvelity?
faqs.a: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember unless it’s close to the time for your next dose. Do not double up doses. Maintain at least 8 hours between doses and avoid taking the second dose too close to bedtime to reduce insomnia.
